issues.legal_issue: Parties to a public interest litigation concerning a public trust may be relegated to an effective statutory forum when the same disputes are pending there and involve complex questions of fact and law.
material_facts: The litigation concerned the public or private character of trust properties, succession to the office of head of the religious institution, and its management.
Statutory inquiries concerning those matters were already pending before the designated authority when the writ petitions were disposed of.
The governing legislation provided procedures for inquiry, findings, appeals, and further adjudication of trust disputes.
The appellant joined the pending statutory proceedings, obtained orders from the authority, and had appeals against those orders pending before the statutory appellate authority.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in relegating the parties to the statutory authority, and the appellant could not pursue the statutory remedy and these appeals simultaneously; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A public interest litigation is ordinarily not the appropriate forum for resolving complex factual and legal disputes concerning management and property of a religious public trust when a self-contained statutory scheme provides an effective forum and the dispute is pending there. The Court relied on Guruvayoor Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan, which states that statutory forums should ordinarily be approached first and that courts should be circumspect in entering disputed matters concerning religious institutions. It also referred to Church of North India v. Lavajibhai Ratanjibhai on the statutory framework and alternative remedies.

rule.if: public_interest_litigation and trust_management_dispute and statutory_inquiry_pending and effective_statutory_forum and disputed_complex_facts and (party_joined_statutory_inquiry or statutory_appeal_pending)

predicates.public_interest_litigation: The proceeding was brought as a public interest litigation.
predicates.trust_management_dispute: The dispute concerned the property, succession, or management of a public trust or religious institution.
predicates.statutory_inquiry_pending: An inquiry into the same dispute was pending before an authority designated by law.
predicates.effective_statutory_forum: The governing legal scheme provided a forum and procedures capable of adjudicating the dispute.
predicates.disputed_complex_facts: Resolving the dispute required determining contested facts and legal issues.
predicates.party_joined_statutory_inquiry: The litigant joined the pending statutory proceeding.
predicates.statutory_appeal_pending: An appeal under the statutory scheme concerning the dispute was pending.

issues.definition: When a public interest litigation concerns disputed trust management matters already within an effective statutory process, and the litigant has pursued that process or its appeal, the court may leave adjudication to that forum.

issues.legal_issue: An authority empowered by the public-trust legislation to conduct inquiries and make findings has jurisdiction to decide disputes about trust property and succession to the trusteeship.
material_facts: The pending statutory inquiries concerned whether disputed properties belonged to the trust and the mode of succession to the office of its head.
The legislation authorized the Assistant Commissioner to inquire into trust status, trust property, trustees, and the mode of succession, and provided for findings and appeals.
The legislation also authorized inquiries and directions concerning trust administration and provided civil-court powers for specified inquiry procedures.
issues.conclusion: The Assistant Commissioner had jurisdiction under the Act to adjudicate the issues raised; the Court rejected the contention that the disputes exceeded that authority’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959 as a self-contained scheme. It relied on Sections 17–24 concerning registration, inquiries, findings, entries, and further inquiries; Sections 38–43 concerning trust administration and appointment of a new working trustee; Section 49 concerning explanations by a working trustee; and Section 67 conferring specified civil-court powers during inquiries. No earlier case was identified as the basis for this jurisdictional holding.

predicates.public_trust_inquiry: The proceeding was an inquiry concerning a public trust under a statutory scheme.
predicates.dispute_concerns_trust_property_or_succe: The dispute concerned whether property belonged to the trust or how succession to a trust office was determined.
predicates.statutory_authority_empowered_to_inquire: The designated authority was legally empowered to investigate the relevant matters and record findings.

issues.definition: When a public-trust inquiry concerns trust property or succession and the designated authority is empowered to investigate and record findings, that authority has jurisdiction to decide the dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A court need not direct the appointment or continuation of a management committee when a challenge to the committee’s constitution is withdrawn with liberty to pursue statutory remedies and appointment of a committee is discretionary.
material_facts: The writ petition challenging the committee was brought by someone other than the appellant.
The petitioner withdrew that writ petition with liberty to raise the issues before the statutory authority, and the appellant did not object or seek to become a party at that time.
The committee’s fixed term had expired several years before the appeals were decided.
The governing provision had been amended so that the Government had discretion, rather than a duty, to appoint a committee.
Orders had been made in the statutory proceedings and appeals against them were pending before the statutory appellate authority.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s dismissal of the writ petition as withdrawn was valid, and the Court declined to direct the Government to appoint a management committee.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 53 of the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959, as amended, appointment of a committee depended on the Government’s satisfaction and discretion; it was not mandatory. The Court also considered that the appellant was not a party to the withdrawn writ petition and had not objected when it was withdrawn. It distinguished the appellant’s reliance on Shehla Burney v. Syed Ali Moosa Raza, observing that the application of a procedural principle depends on the facts and circumstances of the case.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_withdrawal_or_expiry_dismissal and appellant_not_party_to_original_challenge and withdrawal_with_liberty_to_use_statutory_forum and committee_term_expired and government_appointment_discretionary

predicates.appeal_challenges_withdrawal_or_expiry_d: The proceeding was an appeal challenging dismissal of a committee-related case as withdrawn or no longer live after expiry of the committee’s term.
predicates.appellant_not_party_to_original_challeng: The appellant was not a party to the original proceeding challenging the committee.
predicates.withdrawal_with_liberty_to_use_statutory: The original petitioner withdrew the case with permission to raise the issues before the statutory forum.
predicates.committee_term_expired: The management committee’s prescribed term had ended.
predicates.government_appointment_discretionary: The governing law left appointment of a replacement committee to the Government’s discretion.

issues.definition: Where a non-party appellant challenges dismissal after a committee’s term has expired, the original case was withdrawn for recourse to a statutory forum, and replacement appointment is discretionary, the dismissal stands and no appointment direction is required.
